Four ways New York could make a first home cheaper to buy

The city's housing shortage will take years to fix. Its tax on mortgages, the cliffs in its transfer tax and gaps in its sales data could change much sooner.

By Pablo Loschi18 October 2026Updated 15 November 20267 min readSources & methods

Two buyers make offers on the same $900,000 condominium. One pays cash. The other puts 20% down and borrows the remaining $720,000. Recording that loan triggers $13,860 in city and state mortgage recording tax upfront—before any lender credits, exemptions or consolidation breaks. The cash buyer avoids that tax altogether.

What this means for a buyer

In that $900,000 purchase, the $13,860 recording tax adds another 7.7% onto a $180,000 down payment. Other New York taxes jump sharply when a price crosses a dollar threshold. The four proposals below tackle closing costs and public-record blind spots; these records cannot measure how changing them would move home prices or first-time ownership rates.

New York’s deeper problem is a housing shortage that will take years to build out of. The city’s rental vacancy rate was 1.41% in 2023, according to the Housing and Vacancy Survey. On 1 October, the mayor’s administration announced a faster approval route for affordable housing in 12 community districts, due to take effect in January 2027. Those districts produced just 724 of the city’s 63,870 new affordable homes over the preceding five years.

While supply builds slowly, Albany and City Hall can change what buyers pay at closing right away. Linking New York City residential sales from 2016 through 2025 to recorded deeds and mortgages highlights four immediate fixes—none of which replaces building more homes (and public records do not identify which buyers are first-time purchasers).

1. Move the tax off the mortgage

I think it is unfair that a family borrowing to live in a home pays the recording charge while a company buying the same home for cash does not. That is my view, not a finding: the records do not show that every company purchase is speculative, or that every cash buyer lives elsewhere.

For the residential loans in my study, the borrower's rate is 1.80% on loans below $500,000 and 1.925% at or above it, charged on the loan rather than the price. The bigger the loan, the bigger the charge. Loans on co-op shares are not covered, and credits or consolidation agreements can lower a real bill.

The tax could be raised another way. On financed house and condo purchases between $300,000 and $6 million in four boroughs, the recording charge comes to about $248 million a year in my corrected estimate, filling in loan amounts where they are missing. A charge of about 0.872% on every purchase, borrowed or not, would raise the same amount from the same sales. On the $900,000 condo, that is about $7,850 instead of $13,860. Exempting the first $500,000 of each price and charging about 1.55% on the rest would make it about $6,200. The borrowing family would save roughly $6,000 or $7,700, before other adjustments.

Under the schedules I tested, about nine in ten financed purchases would pay less. These figures hold sales and prices fixed, so they do not show that a replacement would bring in the same money in practice. Part of today's tax also goes to the MTA, and any change would have to deal with that. More on the recording tax.

2. Charge each rate on a slice of the price

New York’s “slab” taxes apply a higher rate to the entire amount when a loan or price reaches a threshold. Under the gross schedule, borrowing $500,000 instead of $499,999 adds about $625. At a $1 million residential purchase price, the 1% mansion tax switches on and adds $10,000 relative to a price one dollar below it. Reaching $2 million adds about $5,000 in buyer tax; reaching $5 million adds about $37,500. Exemptions and qualifying older contracts sit outside this illustration.

After higher buyer-tax tiers began at $2 million, $3 million and $5 million in 2019, the share of sales at those exact prices fell by about 60%, while sales just below them climbed. Public records cannot tell us where any individual sale would otherwise have closed, but a comparison against New Jersey points the same way: after New Jersey’s 2004 fee, which exempted sales at exactly $1 million, deals at exactly $1 million still fell 91%. The full story of the $2 million line.

A marginal schedule charges each rate only on the slice of the price above its threshold. England’s stamp duty changed to that structure in December 2014. For New York sales of $2 million or more since 2020, the paper constructs a slice schedule matching the roughly $296 million annual benchmark on those transactions, without one-dollar cliffs. Only about 7% of those high-end sales would pay more under it (holding sales fixed).

3. Check the cash discount before taxing it

A surcharge on all-cash purchases was weighed in May 2026 budget talks and left out of the enacted state budget, according to the city comptroller’s June report. Before lawmakers revive a financing-based tax, it helps to check what the data behind "cash discounts" actually measures.

Repeat sales of the same house do show unfinanced purchases closing about 9% lower. Yet dropping deeds where buyer and seller share a surname shrinks the gap from 9.25 log points (about 9%) to 4.87 log points (roughly 5%)—showing how heavily transaction mix drives the headline number.

Deed filings confirm why. In a stratified sample of 60 transfer reports checked line by line by hand after AI-assisted screening, 16 of 40 same-surname deeds declared a transfer between relatives or another non-market sign, compared with 2 of 20 other cash deeds. When the cash buyer is a company, the price gap is only 1.53 log points (about 1.5%, with a 95% interval from −1.79 to +5.44 log points), leaving a meaningful gap too noisy to pin down. How the cash discount changes.

Replacing the mortgage recording tax with a lower, flat purchase charge that ignores how a buyer pays would remove the asymmetry in the tax law directly. The tradeoffs depend on how prices and borrowing respond, which these historical transactions cannot measure.

4. Publish the deed number and flag non-market transfers

The RP-5217NYC transfer report asks whether a sale is between relatives, involves a buyer who is also a seller, or carries other unusual terms. New York City’s open sales file omits those answers and omits the ACRIS document ID—forcing researchers and buyers to inspect scanned forms one by one.

Linkage rules also deserve public scrutiny: an incorrect unit-lot limit in my early code caused what first looked like a Bronx condo gap, and fixing it raised Bronx condo linkage from 51.7% to 98.8% in release 1.2.0. Read the correction note.

Some foreclosure transfers to lenders also reach the sales file at amounts set by a debt or a legal rule. My deed paper shows that screening them out changes the path of a repeat-sales price index, in a direction that depends on the local rule. It does not give a correction for any single home's value. Clear transfer-condition fields would make these cases easier to spot. Foreclosure deeds in the sales file.

Limits to keep in mind

These proposals concern the bill at closing and the records used to measure the market. They will not build an apartment. Their revenue comparisons hold transactions fixed, and the relationship screens are imperfect. I would still ask lawmakers to explain why borrowing for a home should trigger a charge that paying cash avoids, and to publish the information needed to judge the alternatives.
